newsitem.title: USA: U.S. soybean exports seen dropping sharply - USDA.
newsitem.headline: U.S. soybean exports seen dropping sharply - USDA.

text.p: U.S. soybean exports are expected to drop by a record level in the last half of this marketing year due to plentiful supplies coming out of South America, a senior Agriculture Department analyst told Reuters on Tuesday.

"We're looking at a near record drop in U.S. soybean exports in the last half of the year -- certainly one of the biggest drops we've ever had," said Jim Matthews, chairperson of USDA's soybeans, cottonseed and oils committee of the World Agricultural Outlook Board.
Matthews held out the possibility that USDA could lower its 900-million-bushel soybean export estimate for 1996/97.

"I think it (USDA's export estimate) could go below 900, but it's really difficult to say that at the moment," he said. "We're certainly comfortable with 900, but if prices continue higher, we could see usage drop further here and abroad."

In Tuesday's crop report, USDA left 96/97 soybean ending stocks unchanged at 140 million bushels, and slightly lowered its export estimate to 900 million. The trade had anticipated a drop in ending stocks, and futures prices dropped sharply in reaction to the numbers.

Matthews said the higher ending stocks estimates by the trade were generally because of higher export estimates. But he maintained that bountiful production in South America this year, along with higher U.S. soybean prices, will sharply cut cut into U.S. bean shipments from late March through summer.

"The big thing is the increase in the South American crop ... that will start coming to the market in a more substantial way in late March and April, so they'll start having a pretty big impact on the market in the next two to three weeks," Matthews said in an interview.
The analyst noted that some private trade export estimates put this year's U.S. soybean shipments at 880 million bushels, which he said may end up to be on target.
"If we didn't have a huge stockpile of soybeans in South America, we would go higher with exports and stocks would be lower," Matthews said.
Matthews also said that the strong U.S. dollar could cut further into U.S. soybean exports, especially in Europe where he said prices are already causing a reduction in EU's use of soy products.

Although USDA raised EU's soybean import estimate Tuesday to 14.70 million tonnes from last month's 14.50 million, Matthews said the agency actually lowered soybean meal imports by the EU due to lower meal consumption.
And he said if high prices continue, USDA could lower its EU meal import estimate even more.
"I'm not sure we lowered it enough ... That's a market where we could see a big adjustment," he said.

Although soybean prices were down Tuesday, Matthews did not predict a lasting drop. He said that the big South American supplies have already been factored into the price, and that the key price factor now is this year's U.S. soybean production.

"In the short term, I don't see any reason for any big price break until people are sure about the U.S. crop supplies and plantings ... the only thing that will break the market is more certainty about U.S. crop yields," said Matthews.
